LD 1685: RESOLUTION, Proposing and Amendment to the Constitution of Maine
Concerning the Direct Initiative Process

Sponsor: Representative Amanda Collamore
April 24, 2025

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica, and distinguished members of the Veterans and Legal
Affairs Committee, my name is Amanda Collamore and I have the distinct pleasure of
representing House District 68, Pittsfield, Clinton, Bumham, and Troy. I come before you today
to present LD 1685: RESOLUTION, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine
Concerning the Direct Initiative Process.

This amendment is a targeted, good-government reform aimed at improving our citizen initiative
process while preserving the will of the people and strengthening the Legis1ature's role in responsibly crafting law.

Let me begin by stating clearly: this resolution does not reduce the people's power to bring a
measure forward, and it does not limit the right to referendum. Instead, it ensures that the Legislature can play a meaningful and constructive role in fixing serious problems with an initiative----when those fixes have the broad, bipartisan support of at least two-thirds of both
chambers.

As it currently stands, if a citizens' initiative has clear legal, constitutional, or practical issues----
as many have in recent years---the Legislature is placed in a bind. We are often reluctant to
propose necessary fixes, even with consensus among stakeholders, because doing so automatically creates a competing measure on the ballot. This dual-track process leads to voter confusion and, in some cases, results in no version of the policy ultimately becoming law---even
if the public clearly wants reform.

This resolution provides a path forward for collaboration. If the Legislature believes in the
spirit of an initiative but sees a way to improve it--~through constitutional aligmnent, clearer
language, or broader implementation--it can enact a revised version by a two-thirds vote. That version becomes law without triggering a confusing competing referendum, unless the people themselves demand a vote under the existing constitutional mechanism.

It's worth emphasizing: a two-thirds vote in both chambers is a high bar. It ensures that any
such action is the result of broad, bipartisan consensus. We are not talking about casual tweaks or
partisan substitutions---this is about fixing what needs to be fixed to make initiatives work and
be legally sound, while honoring the intent of the people.

Furthermore, the resolution preserves a clear process for what happens when the Legislature makes changes with less than two-thirds support. In that case, the people will still be presented with both versions of the measure and can choose which one, if any, they prefer. This adds
transparency and choice, while maintaining legislative accountability.
This proposal is about trust---trusting the people, and also trusting this institution to act
responsibly and collaboratively. I believe this amendment strikes that balance.
It does not take away power from the people~"----it simply gives the Legislature the ability to do
what the people elected us to do: improve and enact good law. And it does so without adding confusion at the ballot box or forcing voters to navigate competing proposals when a clear,
broadly supported solution already exists.
For all these reasons, I respectfully urge the Committee to support this resolution and help ensure that Maine's initiative process remains both democratic and functional.
Thank you, and I'd be happy to answer any questions.

Testimony of Shenna Bellows, Secretary of State
And Emily Cook, Deputy Secretary of State
Department of the Secretary of State

April 24, 2025

Testifying neither for not against
L.D. 1685 "RESOLUTION, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine Concerning the
Direct Initiative Process"

Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans
and Legal Affairs, my name is Shenna Bellows, I live in Manchester, and I am the Secretary of State. I am testifying neither for not against L.D. l685.
Maine's citizen initiative process has long been an important way for Maine voters to bring issues to their fellow voters when they believe public support exists for an issue in a way that is not being
validated through the regular legislative process.
In recent years, however, legislators have found themselves wanting or needing to quickly amend new
statute or new statute has been struck down by the courts. We have concerns that voters may feel that
their wishes at the ballot box are not being heeded, and worry that the result of this may be voters
checking out of our electoral process.
We appreciate that Representatives Collamore and Roberts reached out to our office as they started
down the path of introducing L.D. 1685. They are not the first to raise similar ideas, and they
recognized that many concepts raised previously had questions as to their constitutionality. We take no
stance on whether this concept is precisely the one to address our concern regarding potential voter
apathy, but we appreciate their willingness to propose a new idea and keep this conversation going.
Thank you and I would be happy to answer any questions that the committee may have.

Testimony ofRep. Tijfany Roberts in support of
LD 1685, Resolution, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution of Maine
Concerning the Direct Initiative Process
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs
Good afternoon, Senator Hickman, Representative Supica and esteemed members
of the Joint Standing Committee on Veterans and Legal Affairs. I am
Representative Tiffany Roberts, and I represent House District 149, which includes parts of North and South Bervvick. Thank you for the opportunity to testify in
support of LD 1685, Resolution, Proposing an Amendment to the Constitution
of Maine Concerning the Direct Initiative Process.
This is a constitutional amendment that speaks to something I think many of us,
regardless of party or philosophy, are increasingly aware of: our direct initiative process, as foundational and vital as it is, isn't built to handle complex public
policy in its current form.
Mainers are thoughtful, engaged and they show up. They read the questions, they do their homework, and when they head to the polls, they're voting in good faith.
But the reality is, what we put on the ballot isn't always the whole picture. When a
policy is reduced to a single sentence, the nuance, the legal framework, the
unintended consequences -- those are left on the cutting room floor.
We've seen the impact of that. The Right to Repair ballot question passed
overwhelmingly. But what wasn't on the ballot, and what voters couldn't possibly have known, was that the language requires a statewide data access platform that

doesn't exist, to be overseen by an entity that hasn't been named, in a way that
violates federal law. Now we're in a situation where the attorney general is
expected to enforce something that cannot be complied with, and the courts are

being asked to resolve it.

.

That's not good governance. And I don't believe it's What the voters intended.

LD 1685 would amend the Constitution to allow a citizen-initiated measure to
become law without a referendum vote if, and only if -- the Legislature enacts an amended version with a two-thirds vote in both chambers. This doesn't take away the people's power. It ensures that if we, as their elected body, can come together in
a bipartisan supermajority to fix a flawed but well-intentioned policy, we can do so
responsibly and transparently.

It also protects the process. If a proposal is fundamentally changed, or if there's disagreement in the Legislature, it still goes to the ballot, just as it does today. This is not about consolidating power. It's about protecting the integrity of both the initiative process and the laws that result from it.

This is about governing with the tools we need to deliver what Mainers are asking for -- policies that work, rights that are protected and systems that make sense.

Thank you for your time, your consideration and your cormnitment to this work.

I'd be happy to answer any questions.
